comparisons.peer_summary: The income tax benefit decreased to $7.6 billion in 2024 from $8.4 billion in 2023, primarily due to the absence of benefits recorded against pretax charges in 2023 for the FDIC special assessment and the impact of BSBY's cessation.
comparisons.comparison: Both Citi and Bank of America disclosed significant prior-year impacts from FDIC special assessments, noting that 2023 results included large charges that reduced 2024's comparative burden, though Citi reported a direct expense decrease while BAC focused on the tax benefit variance resulting from those charges. Citi noted expenses decreased largely due to a drop in FDIC special assessments from $1.7 billion in 2023 to $203 million in 2024. Bank of America reported that its 2023 income tax benefit included benefits recorded against pretax charges for the FDIC special assessment, which were absent in 2024.

sentences.text: All Other (managed basis) expenses decreased 19%, primarily driven by the lower FDIC special assessment ($203 million in 2024 versus approximately $1.7 billion in the prior year) and a reduction from the closed exits and wind-downs, as well as the lower restructuring charges ($259 million in 2024 versus $781 million in 2023), partially offset by the civil money penalties imposed by the FRB and OCC in July 2024.
The decrease in the income tax benefit was primarily due to the benefits recorded against pretax charges in 2023 for the FDIC special assessment and the impact of BSBY's cessation.

comparisons.peer_summary: Operating expenses decreased 2% to $33.77 billion in 2024, aided by lower CIE commercial real estate impairments and prior year one-time charges like the GreenSky write-down, partially offset by higher compensation and transaction expenses, resulting in an efficiency ratio improvement to 63.1% from 74.6%.
comparisons.comparison: Goldman Sachs and Citi both identified FDIC special assessments as a key driver of expense fluctuations, with Goldman Sachs reporting a prior-year charge of $529 million that contributed to a 2% expense decrease in 2024, while Citi reported a significant drop in FDIC special assessments from $1.7 billion to $203 million contributing to a 19% expense decrease. Both firms cited lower or absent FDIC assessment costs as a primary factor in their 2024 expense trends compared to 2023.

sentences.text: All Other (managed basis) expenses decreased 19%, primarily driven by the lower FDIC special assessment ($203 million in 2024 versus approximately $1.7 billion in the prior year) and a reduction from the closed exits and wind-downs, as well as the lower restructuring charges ($259 million in 2024 versus $781 million in 2023), partially offset by the civil money penalties imposed by the FRB and OCC in July 2024.

Operating expenses were $33.77 billion for 2024, 2% lower than 2023, reflecting decreases driven by significantly lower expenses, including impairments, related to commercial real estate in consolidated investment entities (CIEs) and other significant expenses recognized in the prior year, including the write-down of identifiable intangible assets related to GreenSky Holdings, LLC (GreenSky), an impairment of goodwill related to Consumer platforms and the FDIC special assessment fee.

comparisons.peer_summary: Noninterest expense was $91.8 billion, up 5%, driven by higher compensation and a $1.0 billion Visa share contribution to the foundation, partially offset by lower FDIC-related expenses due to the timing of special assessments.
comparisons.comparison: JPMorgan Chase and Citi both explicitly discussed the impact of FDIC special assessments on noninterest expenses, with JPMorgan noting a decrease in FDIC-related expense due to the timing of a $2.9 billion assessment in 2023 versus a $725 million increase in 2024, while Citi highlighted a decrease in FDIC special assessments from $1.7 billion to $203 million. Both disclosures attribute part of their expense variance to the normalization or timing of these regulatory fees.

sentences.text: All Other (managed basis) expenses decreased 19%, primarily driven by the lower FDIC special assessment ($203 million in 2024 versus approximately $1.7 billion in the prior year) and a reduction from the closed exits and wind-downs, as well as the lower restructuring charges ($259 million in 2024 versus $781 million in 2023), partially offset by the civil money penalties imposed by the FRB and OCC in July 2024.

• Noninterest expense was $91.8 billion, up 5%, driven by higher compensation expense, including higher revenue-related compensation and growth in the number of employees, as well as a $1.0 billion contribution of Visa shares to the JPMorgan Chase Foundation recorded in the second quarter of 2024, partially offset by lower FDIC-related expense, reflecting a $2.9 billion special assessment recognized in the fourth quarter of 2023, compared with a $725 million increase to the FDIC special assessment recognized in the first quarter of 2024.

comparisons.peer_summary: Wealth Management non-interest expenses increased 5% to $20,618 million in 2024 compared to the prior year. This increase was driven by higher compensation and benefits expenses, primarily due to increased formulaic payouts to representatives on higher compensable revenues, partially offset by decreases in non-compensation expenses such as professional services, legal expenses, and FDIC special assessment costs.
comparisons.comparison: Morgan Stanley and Citi both identified lower FDIC special assessment costs as a contributing factor to their 2024 expense trends compared to 2023. Morgan Stanley reported that lower FDIC special assessment costs helped offset increases in non-compensation expenses within its Wealth Management segment, while Citi cited the reduction in FDIC special assessments from $1.7 billion to $203 million as a primary driver for a 19% decrease in All Other expenses.
